Vs.

full_judgment:
2. The Rule was issued to show cause as to why the order dated 23.7.86 passed by the learned Sessions Judge and Special Tribunal Judge, Rajshahi in Special Tribunal Case No. 1 of 1986 admitting Exts. 4, 5 and 6 series into evidence should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper and pending hearing of the Rule, all further proceedings of Special Tribunal Case No. 1 of 1986, now pending in the court of Sessions Judge and Special Tribunal Judge, Rajshahi was stayed. This Rule was issued by this court in August, 1986. 

 4. The Special Tribunal recorded the testimony of the witnesses when certain objection was taken as to the admission and marking of certain Exts. in the instant case being Ext. Nos. 3, 4 and 5 the alleged confessional statement of the accused into evidence. Being rejected it was challenged before this court and a Rule was obtained when all further proceedings had been stayed. 

 5. Mr. Lutfur Rahman Mondal, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner in support of the Rule, having taken us through the confessional statements in original from the records which had been called by the special messenger from Rangpur, submitted that the learned Magistrate acted without jurisdiction in recording the confessional statement without following strictly the provisions as contained in section 164(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The confessional statement must be recorded observing the mandatory provision of section 164 CrPC and that of the High Court Rules 23 and 84 and where the confessional statements had not been recorded as under the law the said would be inadmissible. The learned Counsel has referred to the Privy Council decision which had been followed thereafter by the courts of this subcontinent and has also referred to the decision of this court in the case of Zeheda Bewa & another Vs. The State reported in 37 DLR at page 66 and submitted that it has been held consistently by the court of this sub-continent following the decision of the Privy Council that a plain paper statement by an accused recorded by the Magistrate without strictly following the provision of the Criminal Procedure Code would render the confessional statement unworthy of credit and not admissible in evidence and that a Magistrate subsequently deposing to the fact of voluntariness or otherwise of the confessional statement would not cure that initial illegality. 

 6. Section 164 CrPC provided that any Magistrate of the 1st Class or of the second class specially empowered in this behalf may record any statement or confession made to him in course of investigation or at any time afterwards but before completion of the enquiry and the trial. Any such statement be recorded by such Magistrate in the presence of the accused and be recorded in such manner prescribed for recording evidence as in his opinion best fitted for the circumstances of the case and such statement of confession be recorded and signed and then be forwarded to the Magistrate by whom the case is to be tried. It has been further provided that the Magistrate shall before recording any such confession explain to the person making it that he is not bound to make a confession and that if he would make do so it may be used as evidence against him and no Magistrate shall record any such confession unless upon questioning the person making it he has reasons to believe that it was made voluntarily and after he recorded the confession shay make a memorandum thus:- 

 I have explained to the accused that he is not bound to make a confession and that if he does so any confession he may make, may be used as evidence against him and I believe that this confession was voluntarily made. It was taken in my presence and hearing and was read over to the person making it and admitted by , him to be correct and it contains a full and true account of the statement made by him." 

 10. From a reading of the confessional exhibits it is seen that after recording the confessional statements the Magistrate recorded that after having questioned the accused he believed that the statements as recorded are voluntary. This has been objected to on the ground that the questions put by the Magistrate and the answers given by the accused had not been narrated and that being so it cannot be found by the trial Court that the statements were voluntary. We find no substance in that contention also as only because the actual questions and answers had not been narrated it would not be said that the Magistrate's opinion of voluntariness of the statement would not go into evidence to be examined by the court. 

 11. Section 164 CrPC provides for recording the statement made by an accused. The accused is not to be questioned as if cross examined but he he asked by the Magistrate only to give or narrate whatever he wants to say in his own way, after giving him a warning that he is not bound to make any such statement and if made it would be used against him. The Magistrate in recording so must also be satisfied that the accused had made the statement voluntarily at the time it was made in his presence. For those purposes a printed form is used, as directed, by the Magistrate where the question are already there printed for Magistrate's guidance but when such a printed form is not used, may be for its non-availability as is often the case or by mistake, a statement only in a plain papers without narrating the questions put and the answers given, would not by itself make the said record inadmissible in evidence. 

 13. We are in respectful agreement with the above and conclude by adding that the memorandum or the certificate given by the Magistrate as to what had happened, how he warned, gave time for reflection, how yet the accused insisted in making the statement and how he read over the statement made to the accused and his admitting those to be correct and the Magistrate's believing those to be voluntary, ought to be treated as conclusive evidence of the facts stated therein unless shown to be otherwise before the Court.
